chapters.title: Executive Brief
chapters.guidingQuestion: What should I understand in my first ten minutes?
chapters.headline: A $3.42B technology spend is 60% outsourced, its flagship transformation programs are barely off the ground, and leadership already agrees—unanimously—that value isn't being proven fast enough.
chapters.executive_synthesis: In your first ten minutes: this is an $81.4B carrier where technology is 4.2% of revenue, $2.05B of which is run through third parties—enough to make vendor management a core discipline, not overhead. The transformation portfolio meant to modernize the business—Meridian integration, NDC, contact-center migration, data platform migration—sits at single-digit-to-low-teens completion. That stall matters because all 26 interviewed leaders independently flagged value realization and investment priority as concerns, and the AI portfolio backs that sentiment with a hard number: only 7% ($5.7M of $80.2M) of promised value is finance-validated. Layered onto this is a live, high-severity security gap—standing privileged credentials outside CyberArk PAM coverage—and Meridian's own legacy-reconciliation risk, which may be facets of the same integration problem given the program's 7% completion and slipped platform migration. A flagged $210.0M pool of replacement-candidate applications is worth examining as a possible funding source, though no direct linkage is established. Net: stalled execution, unproven value, and real risk exposure demand direct executive attention now.

key_insights.statement: This is an $81.4B, 92,000-employee network carrier where technology represents 4.2% of revenue ($3.42B), and 60% of that spend ($2.05B) is contracted to third parties—a level of outsourcing that suggests vendor management could warrant treatment as a core operating discipline rather than a back-office function.

Nearly the entire strategic transformation portfolio — Meridian integration (7%), NDC (11%), contact-center migration (9%), and data platform migration (12%) — is running at single-digit-to-low-teens percent completion.
All 26 interviewed leaders raised value realization and investment priority as concerns — this is enterprise-wide consensus, not a pocket of dissatisfaction.
The AI portfolio has validated only 7% of its promised value ($5.7M of $80.2M) through finance, a concrete number behind the leadership sentiment on value realization.
A high-severity privileged-access security gap exists: standing privileged credentials remain outside CyberArk PAM coverage. This is a named, live exposure, not a theoretical one.

tensions.statement: The Meridian integration program's 7% completion and explicit platform-migration block deserve direct executive review, since this is both a named strategic priority and the source of two named high-severity risks.

Given 117 applications ($210.0M) already flagged as replacement candidates, management should examine whether rationalizing this subset could help fund parts of the stalled modernization portfolio, though the packet does not establish a direct funding linkage.

The near-universal leadership concern about value realization (26 of 26 interviewed leaders raised it), paired with the 7% AI value-validation rate ($5.7M finance-validated against $80.2M promised), suggests a gap between claimed and confirmed value that finance and program governance may want to address before further AI or transformation investment decisions are made.

what_to_watch.statement: Standing privileged credentials outside PAM coverage is rated a high-severity risk tied to CyberArk PAM. The status of the remediation effort is not established by the available facts.

Meridian Regional legacy systems being unreconciled with mainline is rated high severity, tied to Meridian Legacy Sabre DCS. Given that the Meridian Regional Technology Integration Program is only 7% complete and blocked on a platform migration slipped two quarters, these two issues could be related facets of the same underlying integration challenge, though the facts don't explicitly confirm a direct link.

chapters.title: Our Business
chapters.guidingQuestion: How does this enterprise work and create value?
chapters.headline: Value creation centers on Airport & Ground Operations, which is technology-intensive and increasingly dependent on a concentrated set of third-party vendors for both digital infrastructure and physical service delivery.
chapters.executive_synthesis: This enterprise's operational core sits in Airport & Ground Operations, which carries the largest technology footprint of any measured area — 217 applications and $466.7M in annual spend — underscoring its centrality to how value is delivered. That value creation is not purely internal: 60% of the total $3.42B technology budget flows to third-party contractors, with a single vendor, SITA, representing 13.9% ($285.0M) of that spend in direct support of ground operations. Physical operations follow the same pattern, with outstation ground handling and catering run through named outsourced providers (Menzies/Swissport, Gate Gourmet/dnata). Together these observations suggest an enterprise that creates value by orchestrating a dense web of technology and vendor relationships around its ground operations rather than performing all functions in-house. Management's stated growth priorities — NDC/direct distribution and AI-assisted disruption recovery — suggest the next value levers are commercial distribution control and operational resilience, though the precise extent of vendor-dependency risk is not established by the figures alone.

key_insights.statement: Airport & Ground Operations carries by far the largest technology footprint (217 applications, $466.7M annually) of any area measured.

Growth priorities — scaling NDC/direct distribution and AI-assisted disruption recovery — indicate management sees commercial distribution control and operational resilience, not just capacity, as the next levers of value.

60% of the $3.42B technology budget is third-party contracted spend ($2.05B), and a single vendor (SITA) accounts for 13.9% ($285.0M) of that vendor base, supporting Airport & Ground Operations — this concentration could suggest some degree of dependency on key external vendors, though the extent of operational exposure isn't established by these figures alone.

Outstation ground handling and catering — core operational functions — are run through named third-party managed services (Menzies/Swissport at $74.5M/yr, Gate Gourmet/dnata at $62.0M/yr), indicating reliance on outsourced vendors for physical operations.

limitations: Segment-level revenue and profitability economics are not represented in the packet's business context, limiting the value_creation_model to technology-dependency framing rather than a full economic picture.

chapters.title: Strategy & Value Creation
chapters.guidingQuestion: Where are we trying to go, and what bets are we making?
chapters.headline: The company's declared bets — Meridian integration, a $457.4M value portfolio, and AI/platform modernization — are consistently running behind their own timelines, adoption targets, and financial validation.
chapters.executive_synthesis: The strategic direction is clear enough: finish the Meridian Regional integration, capture $457.4M of expected value from a $407.4M program portfolio, and modernize the data and AI platform. But the evidence shows each bet trailing its own ambition. Meridian integration, a top priority, is only 7% complete and blocked by a slipped migration. The portfolio's 1.12x return is management-declared, not finance-confirmed, echoing a broader pattern of AI value claims outrunning validated results — visible in stalled pilots with no owner for rollout or funding, and in Copilot and Crew Recovery AI adoption running 26 points below target. Even where automation opportunity has been identified, as with Contact Center Workforce Forecasting, deployment remains minimal. Layered on top, governance friction is named by nearly all leaders as a burden, raised as often as capability gaps, suggesting the organization may be spending governance effort without confidence it is building the capability these bets require — though that causal link is not directly established.

key_insights.statement: Completing the Meridian Regional integration is a declared top priority, but the flagship program measuring that integration is only 7% complete and explicitly blocked by a slipped platform migration — the bet is materially behind its own implied timeline.

The declared program portfolio shows $407.4M of budget against $457.4M of expected value (a 1.12x declared return across 38 programs), but this return is management-declared and not yet finance-confirmed, which is consistent with the low finance-validation rate seen in the AI-specific value tracking.

tensions.statement: Leadership consistently names governance friction as a burden (architecture review cited by one CEO as adding six weeks with little effect on outcomes), and this theme was raised by 24 of 26 leaders — the same breadth as capability_gap, also raised by 24 of 26. This overlap could suggest governance is experienced as a cost that leadership is not confident is buying capability improvement, though the interviews don't directly establish that causal link.

Contact Center Workforce Forecasting is rated a High automation candidate but runs only 2% automation with a 6.8% error rate — a case that could point to a gap between identified automation opportunity and deployed capability, worth checking against other High-rated processes.

A declared strategic priority (data and AI platform modernization) sits against measured underperformance in adoption: Microsoft 365 Copilot and Crew Recovery AI are both 26 points below their adoption targets.

AI pilots stalling after proof-of-concept, cited by 15 of 26 leaders and echoed directly in testimony about a pilot with no owner for operational rollout or ongoing funding, is consistent with the wide gap between promised and finance-validated AI value.

chapters.title: How We Operate
chapters.guidingQuestion: How is the enterprise organized and how does work get done?
chapters.headline: The enterprise's operations run through a small set of legacy systems and an even smaller set of specialists who understand them, creating key-person and platform-concentration risk.
chapters.executive_synthesis: Work in this enterprise moves through a handful of critical systems, and the evidence suggests operational continuity leans heavily on narrow pockets of expertise rather than broad, resilient capability. The CA-7 batch scheduler, central to core operations on the mainframe, is flagged as a high-severity risk precisely because the skills needed to run it are concentrated in a small, aging group. Similarly, risk and control exposure is not evenly spread across the technology estate: the Meridian Legacy Finance System and ServiceNow CMDB each surface repeatedly across separate risk entries, marking them as focal points of operational fragility. At the process level, contact center throughput is reportedly bottlenecked by a small number of engineers able to safely change one core cargo booking system, showing that even routine pace of change can hinge on a few individuals. Together these observations point to an operating model where continuity and change both depend disproportionately on a limited set of systems and people, though the available evidence does not establish how widespread this pattern is beyond these specific cases.

key_insights.statement: Mainframe skills concentration is rated a high-severity risk tied to the CA-7 batch scheduler, meaning the platform underpinning core operations depends on a narrow, aging skills base.

Two systems — the Meridian Legacy Finance System and ServiceNow CMDB — are each named in two separate risk or control entries, a modest but real concentration of declared risk exposure onto specific systems.

Contact center throughput is reportedly constrained by a small number of engineers who can safely change one core cargo booking system, suggesting key-person dependency limits the pace of change in at least one operational system.

chapters.title: Technology & Data
chapters.guidingQuestion: What enables the business, and where is complexity or dependency concentrated?
chapters.headline: Core data and infrastructure platforms are running one to two maturity levels below target, with governance, migration progress, and capacity headroom all lagging what the business needs to move faster.
chapters.executive_synthesis: Technology enablement is uneven: several foundational data and AI platforms — Snowflake, Databricks, Confluent Kafka, and Informatica — each sit one maturity level below their stated targets, and the Teradata-to-Snowflake migration meant to help close that gap is only 12% complete. Governance is further behind, with Collibra two levels below target and data catalog coverage flagged as a medium risk, pointing to stewardship gaps beyond technology alone. Underscoring this, none of the 183 declared evidence sources are yet approved for loading, suggesting the analytical foundation isn't fully operational, even though the explicit regulated-data footprint appears modest (58 of 632 assets). Meanwhile, nearly a quarter of the application estate ($210M, 117 apps) is already flagged for replacement, and tier-1-critical infrastructure — the primary data center, mainframe, and private cloud cluster — runs with thin capacity headroom and only warm-tier disaster recovery. Together these point to dependency concentrated in aging, capacity-constrained infrastructure and in unfinished platform and governance modernization.

key_insights.statement: Several data and AI platform components each sit one maturity level below their stated target: Snowflake (Platform Architecture & Scalability, 4 vs. target 5), Databricks Lakehouse (AI/ML & Automation Enablement, 3 vs. target 4), Confluent Kafka (Platform Architecture & Scalability, 3 vs. target 4), and Informatica PowerCenter (Platform Architecture & Scalability, 2 vs. target 3). Separately, the Teradata to Snowflake Migration Program is only 12% complete, which could be a contributing factor to these gaps, though the facts don't establish a direct link between the migration funding and all four platforms' maturity shortfalls.

Collibra Data Governance & Stewardship sits two maturity levels below target (2 vs. 4), and data catalog coverage below the governance target is independently flagged as a medium-severity risk — together suggesting stewardship gaps, not just platform technology, may be limiting progress here.
183 of 183 declared evidence sources are not yet approved for loading, which could suggest the analytical and governance foundation intended to support faster decision-making is not yet operational.

Only 58 of 632 tracked data assets/integrations carry regulated data, a relatively small explicit regulated footprint, though this figure alone should not be assumed to reflect overall data-risk exposure.

tensions.statement: 23% of the application estate (117 applications, $210.0M) is already flagged as replacement candidates, indicating a meaningful share of the technology estate is being carried past its useful strategic life.

Multiple tier-1-critical infrastructure platforms — the primary data center, the mainframe LPAR, and the private cloud VMware cluster — operate with low remaining capacity headroom (16%-53%) and only warm-tier disaster recovery, constraining both operational resilience and the pace of workload migration off them.

chapters.title: Performance & Value
chapters.guidingQuestion: Are we moving toward outcomes, and can we prove the value?
chapters.headline: Value tracking is lagging investment ambition: only 7% of promised AI value has been finance-confirmed, and nearly half the tracked metrics can't even be verified.
chapters.executive_synthesis: The evidence does not yet support a confident claim that outcomes are being realized at the pace investment suggests. AI initiatives promised $80.2M in value but only $5.7M has been finance-confirmed—7%—a gap far starker than the broader portfolio's declared 1.12x return, itself unconfirmed by finance. Underlying this is a data-quality problem: 11 of 26 tracked metrics lack comparable baselines, targets, and actuals, and 9 more mix notation, meaning much of what looks like performance cannot currently be verified. None of the 65 declared vendor contracts have supporting documents in this packet, further limiting independent corroboration. Leadership testimony reinforces the concern directly, citing a modernization program whose approved benefit number was never revisited, though most sentiment cannot be tied to specific named programs. Adoption shortfalls in AI tools suggest workforce uptake, not just technical deployment, may also constrain value capture. Together, these point to ambition outrunning proof, not proof of failure or success.

key_insights.statement: AI value realization is confirmed at only 7% of what was promised ($5.7M of $80.2M), an outcome gap far larger than the general 1.12x declared portfolio return would suggest.

11 of 26 tracked metrics lack a comparable baseline, target, and actual, and 9 of the comparable set mix notation — meaning a substantial share of claimed performance cannot currently be verified, a data-quality gap rather than a performance result.

None of the 65 declared vendor contracts have document-level evidence behind them in this packet, so vendor terms, renewal dates, and obligations cited elsewhere (e.g., the SITA renewal window) cannot be independently corroborated from contract documents.

tensions.statement: The AI portfolio shows a stark promised-versus-validated value gap ($80.2M promised, $5.7M finance-confirmed, 7%), while the broader program portfolio separately declares a 1.12x return ($407.4M budget vs. $457.4M expected value across 38 programs) that is itself not yet finance-confirmed. Together, these two gaps could suggest value tracking discipline is lagging investment ambition, though this pattern is not yet established beyond these two data points.

Leadership testimony directly states that a modernization program's approved benefit number was never revisited to check whether it landed — an example consistent with the broader value-realization concern that was raised by all 26 interviewed leaders, though it's not established that others referenced this specific case.

AI tool adoption is running well below target (Copilot and Crew Recovery AI both 26 points below adoption target), which could suggest that even where AI capability has been deployed, workforce uptake — not just technical readiness — may be limiting value capture.

Program-specific leadership sentiment can only be resolved to a canonical program in 9.6% of interview mentions, so the enterprise-wide value-realization concern cannot be reliably attributed to specific named programs beyond the few where an explicit link exists (e.g., the CEO's direct reference to Infrastructure & Cloud Modernization Program).

questions_to_ask: Both Microsoft 365 Copilot and Crew Recovery AI are running 26 points below their adoption targets. What's driving this shared shortfall — whether training, workflow, or trust issues — is worth investigating.
limitations: 11 of 26 tracked metrics lack a comparable baseline/target/actual set, and 9 of the comparable 15 mix notation, meaning roughly half of the metric portfolio cannot support a confident performance claim.

chapters.title: Leadership Perspective
chapters.guidingQuestion: What do leaders agree on, disagree on, and worry about?
chapters.headline: Leaders show near-total consensus on value realization, investment priority, governance friction, capability gaps, manual effort, data trust, and vendor dependency — but perception diverges from documented system fact in a material minority of cases.
chapters.executive_synthesis: Across 26 interviews, leadership agreement is unusually strong: every leader raised value realization and investment priority, and near-unanimous majorities flagged governance friction, capability gaps, manual effort, data trust, and vendor dependency. This breadth suggests these are shared structural concerns rather than isolated gripes. On vendor dependency specifically, system data showing SITA at 13.9% of vendor spend offers plausible context, though the evidence does not establish a direct causal link. Disagreement, by contrast, is limited to a couple of individually-held views — one leader's concern about shelfware, another's about a narrowing renewal window — with no corroboration from peers, marking these as personal rather than collective positions. The clearest worry for the organization is not any single theme but a reliability gap: 81 of 586 leadership statements contradict system-of-record evidence on the same topics, meaning leaders' perceptions, however consensual, cannot be assumed to match documented fact and should be verified rather than taken at face value.

key_insights.statement: Value realization and investment priority were each raised by all 26 interviewed leaders — a full consensus view on both themes, not an isolated opinion.
Governance friction and capability gaps were each raised by 24 of 26 leaders, near-unanimous concerns.
Manual effort and data trust were each raised by 23 of 26 leaders, indicating broad agreement that core data and process reliability is a live problem, not a one-off complaint.

Vendor dependency was raised by 22 of 26 leaders, a consensus view. Separately, system data shows SITA represents 13.9% of total vendor spend ($285.0M of $2.05B), supporting Airport & Ground Operations — a concentration that may be relevant context for those concerns, though the data does not directly link the two.

tensions.statement: The themes shelfware and renewal leverage were each raised by only one leader, with no corroboration elsewhere in the interview set — indicating these are individual observations (a CFO on underused licensing, a distribution VP on a narrowing vendor renewal window) rather than shared leadership positions.

81 of 586 leadership interview statements contradict the system-of-record evidence on the same topic, meaning leadership perception and documented system fact diverge in a material minority of cases and should not be treated as interchangeable.

chapters.title: What Needs Attention
chapters.guidingQuestion: What tensions, risks, dependencies and decisions deserve executive attention?
chapters.headline: Executive attention should center on the stalled Meridian integration program, whose 7% completion and platform-migration block sit at the root of multiple high-severity risks and an unresolved value-realization gap across AI and transformation spend.
chapters.executive_synthesis: The most urgent item is the Meridian Regional Technology Integration Program: 7% complete, blocked on a slipped platform migration, and linked to two named high-severity risks, including unreconciled Meridian Legacy Sabre DCS systems that may share the same root cause. Standing privileged credentials outside PAM coverage and mainframe skills concentration on CA-7 add further high-severity exposure, compounded by a tier1-critical mainframe running at 27% headroom with only warm DR. Financially, 117 replacement-candidate applications worth $210.0M raise an unconfirmed but worth-examining question of whether rationalization could help fund stalled modernization. Meanwhile, near-unanimous leadership concern over value realization, against only 7% of promised AI value being finance-validated, suggests governance should tighten before further investment. A three-year-accepted M&A recovery-position risk, per CEO testimony, and SITA vendor concentration with a narrow renewal window round out the decisions warranting direct executive oversight.
